answer: 'NoSQL' throws everything not MySQL/Postgres/Oracle under one blanket (like 'technical/non-technical'); name the type/database. 'NoSQL scales' as blanket is wrong: you can build a non-relational DB that doesn't scale; those that scale, scale for a specific workload (Cassandra writes, DynamoDB key lookups).
They give up consistency to get scalability and availability.
evidence: §1.4 'give up consistency to get scalability and availability'

answer: ACID consistency (correctness: each transaction moves data valid state to valid state) and CAP consistency (visibility/linearizability: a read after a write returns it). NoSQL gives up the CAP one (strong consistency).
A single relational primary without a standby takes everything down when it fails; data spread over replicated nodes keeps serving when one fails. Result: eventual consistency.
'NoSQL DBs scale does not mean SQL does not → anything that shards, scales.' Backed by Lecture 3's KV store on MySQL split by key range A–M / N–Z behind a router.

A document database, because it is close to relational in power; you'll almost never see a jump straight to a KV store (too restrictive: no queries inside the value).
Changing one attribute of one document and nothing else ($set). In a blob KV store you read the whole value, change it in code and write the whole value back.
DynamoDB: a KV store that also supports a document model (filter on nested attributes). Focus on the features you need (complex queries, partial updates) and pick the DB that gives them.
MongoDB started out 'BASE, not ACID' and now supports ACID transactions.
Only key-wise operations: get, put, delete a key, add member to set at a key; never peek into the value. Examples: Redis, DynamoDB, Aerospike.

Every KV operation names one key so lands on exactly one shard; richer queries (range, IN) may touch many shards and wait for the slowest, which is very expensive, so they can't be split thousands of ways.

Restrictive: only key-wise access, useless unless use case fits; in exchange massive partitioning/parallelism (thousands of partitions). 'The more complex the queries, the less you can distribute the data.'
